rule: State the strongest conclusion supported by the evidence while preserving proposition boundaries and residual uncertainty.

assessments.text: Iran's conventional navy suffered catastrophic losses; this does not mean every IRGC small craft was destroyed.
basis: CSIS open-source/satellite assessment documents near-total conventional surface-fleet loss.
AP reports more than 90% of the regular navy lost while noting Revolutionary Guard small attack boats remained.

assessments.text: The CAOC was knocked out. Al Udeid was not.
basis: Multiple Iranian missiles rendered the CAOC inoperable.
The air campaign continued through preplanned distributed command at Shaw; the record does not establish whole-base incapacity.

assessments.text: Iran shot down the F-15E. The subsequent personnel-recovery mission succeeded. Claims that it was actually a uranium-seizure raid remain unsupported.
basis: Canonical chain corrects the initial F-35 identification to F-15E.
Both crew were recovered; disabled recovery aircraft were destroyed by U.S. forces to prevent capture.
A separate uranium contingency existed, but no operation-specific evidence links it to the rescue.

assessments.text: Iran suffered severe senior-leadership disruption, including the Supreme Leader and multiple senior security-command figures; the state nevertheless continued to function and replace leadership.
basis: The accepted itemized leadership ledger contains a canonical minimum of 11 individually identified senior political/state and military/security deaths.
Later Iranian diplomacy and military activity demonstrate state and command continuity after the losses.

assessments.text: Iran's conventional force was severely attrited across aircraft, launchers, air defense/radar and naval assets; surviving missile/UAS capacity means this was degradation, not disarmament.
basis: Accepted floors include 23+ aircraft and 58+ naval losses.
335+ launchers are reported neutralized; neutralized is not silently converted to destroyed.
Standing missile-inventory modeling retains the accepted 833 / 1,417 / 3,000 replacement-equivalent scenarios and separates physical loss/damage from temporary inaccessibility.

assessments.text: Iran retained mediation channels and bargaining relevance but did not convert pressure into a durable final settlement; several regional security relationships hardened rather than fracturing.
basis: Omani, Pakistani and other mediation channels remained active.
Repeated interim arrangements did not produce a durable final settlement by the canonical cutoff.
Regional alignment records show increased security coordination while preserving partner disagreement over specific U.S. proposals.

assessments.text: On force preservation, the current public record favors the U.S./coalition: Iran absorbed substantially deeper durable conventional-force attrition while coalition campaign-generating capacity remained broadly intact.
basis: Iranian standing-loss categories now provide enough itemized depth for a comparative assessment.
U.S./coalition losses and local facility damage were material, including the Al Udeid CAOC loss, but did not produce equivalent theater-wide conventional-force attrition.
Iran retained consequential missile/UAS, small-craft and Hormuz coercive capability, limiting any stronger claim.

assessments.text: Iran retained high de facto Hormuz coercive and sea-denial leverage, but that did not become recognized exclusive sovereignty or an accepted compulsory toll regime.
basis: Canonical shipping and maritime records show sustained suppression of normal commercial traffic and meaningful selective-routing leverage.
The evidence distinguishes practical gatekeeping from legal sovereignty and durable monetizable rent.

assessments.text: Iranian pressure did not consistently fracture regional alignment and in several cases accelerated security, economic and route-diversification coordination, although partners did not uniformly join every U.S. military initiative.
basis: Regional coalition, defense and economic records show harder coordination in response to maritime and missile risk.
Oman and other mediators continued engagement with Iran, and participation in proposed navigation missions remained uneven.
